observation.visible_scene: A close, top-down view of two round brilliant-cut faceted gemstones sitting side by side on a white, finely textured surface with horizontal ridges. Two circular recesses are visible along the top edge of the frame. The stones are stationary: the left stone stays centered near the left half and the right stone near the right half throughout, with no translation, no rotation of the facet pattern (the kite/"arrowhead" facet at the top of each stone remains pointing up), and no contact between them. The camera and background appear essentially fixed.
visible_changes: The play of light across both stones changes continuously: bright white specular flashes and small colored (orange, blue, purple) internal reflections shift position and intensity from frame to frame within each stone, while the stones themselves do not move.

The right stone consistently produces a strong vertical lens-flare beam rising from its top toward the upper recess; its brightness and the shape of the central starburst vary, and at several points (e.g. mid-clip and near the end) a distinct blue/violet 'V' or chevron of fire appears in its center.

The left stone's highlights move around its face—e.g. an orange flash at the upper-left and a white flash at the upper-right in some frames, a broad white flash at the lower-center in others—sometimes accompanied by faint vertical flare streaks above it.

The overall pattern of brilliance cycles through similar states (dim internal sparkle vs. bright starburst with colored fire) across the excerpt, but the first and last frames do not line up as an identical loop.
outside_clip_unknowns: What produces the changing reflections is not visible: it could be a moving light source, a rotating stage, or a moving camera, none of which can be confirmed from these frames alone.
Whether this excerpt is part of a longer continuous rotation/display sequence is unknown.
uncertain_details: Any camera motion (slight drift or zoom) is uncertain because the textured background and ridge positions look effectively constant.
The material identity of the stones (diamond vs. simulant) cannot be determined from the images.
The exact facet orientation of each stone is hard to read under the glare, so subtle rotation, if any, cannot be fully ruled out.
